# Consumer Behavior and Branding {#consumer-behavior}

In April 1985 the Coca-Cola Company replaced the formula of its flagship drink
with a sweeter recipe that had beaten both the original and Pepsi in extensive
blind taste tests. The launch of "New Coke" provoked letters, protests, and a
wave of press coverage, and within three months the company brought the
original back as Coca-Cola Classic. Consumers had rejected a product they
preferred when they could not see the label. The episode is the most famous
demonstration of a point this chapter develops at length: what consumers buy is
rarely just a bundle of physical attributes. They buy expectations that can be
met or disappointed, chains of meaning that link attributes to personal values,
memories of a brand, a partner in a relationship, a mirror for the self, a
licence to indulge, a feeling of "mine", a reference point against which a
price feels fair, and a share in a culture.

Similar puzzles appear across categories. Why do some owners of Harley-Davidson
motorcycles tattoo the company's logo on their skin, while few owners of
equally reliable machines feel any such loyalty? Why did Porsche's move into
sport utility vehicles succeed while Bic's move from pens and lighters into
perfume did not? Why do shoppers at outlet malls respond to "compare at" prices
that they may not fully believe, and why did a large US department store chain
lose customers when it abolished the discounts that its shoppers claimed to
dislike? Why does touching a mug in a store make it feel more valuable, and why
do people choose less-preferred options "for the sake of variety"?

This chapter introduces twelve theories that consumer researchers and brand
managers use to answer such questions. We begin with the cognitive core of
post-purchase evaluation (**[expectancy-disconfirmation](#expectancy-disconfirmation)**) and the
motivational logic linking product features to personal values (**means-end
chain theory**). We then turn to the brand: how it lives in consumer memory
(**[customer-based brand equity](#customer-based-brand-equity)**), how it acquires human characteristics
(**[brand personality](#brand-personality)**), how consumers form relationships with it
(**[consumer-brand relationships](#consumer-brand-relationships)**), and how it expresses the self
(**[self-congruity](#self-congruity)**). Four theories address how consumers evaluate and choose:
**schema congruity** (new products and brand extensions), the
**hedonic-utilitarian** distinction, **[psychological ownership](#psychological-ownership)**, and
**[variety seeking](#variety-seeking)**. Two final theories widen the lens to price perception
(**[reference price](#reference-price)**) and to the cultural meanings of consumption
(**[consumer culture theory](#consumer-culture-theory)**). Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-glance) summarises the
territory.

```{r tab-cb-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "[Expectancy-disconfirmation](#expectancy-disconfirmation)", "How do consumers judge whether they are satisfied?", "Individual", "Oliver (1980)",
  "[Means-end chain](#means-end-chain)", "How do product attributes connect to personal values?", "Individual", "Gutman (1982)",
  "[Customer-based brand equity](#customer-based-brand-equity)", "Why does the same marketing work better for some brands?", "Individual / brand", "Keller (1993), Aaker (1991)",
  "[Brand personality](#brand-personality)", "Which human traits do consumers ascribe to brands?", "Brand", "Aaker (1997)",
  "[Consumer-brand relationships](#consumer-brand-relationships)", "Can consumers have relationships with brands, and of what kind?", "Dyad (consumer-brand)", "Fournier (1998)",
  "[Self-congruity](#self-congruity)", "Why do consumers prefer brands that match who they are?", "Individual", "Sirgy (1982), Belk (1988)",
  "[Schema congruity](#schema-congruity)", "Why are moderately unexpected products evaluated favourably?", "Individual", "Meyers-Levy & Tybout (1989)",
  "[Hedonic and utilitarian consumption](#hedonic-utilitarian)", "How do pleasure and function shape choice and justification?", "Individual", "Hirschman & Holbrook (1982), Dhar & Wertenbroch (2000)",
  "[Psychological ownership](#psychological-ownership)", "Why do people value what feels like theirs?", "Individual", "Pierce, Kostova & Dirks (2001)",
  "[Variety seeking](#variety-seeking)", "Why do consumers switch away from a favourite?", "Individual", "McAlister & Pessemier (1982)",
  "[Reference price](#reference-price)", "Against what standard do consumers judge a price?", "Individual / market", "Winer (1986), Mazumdar et al. (2005)",
  "[Consumer culture theory](#consumer-culture-theory)", "How do consumers use goods and brands to make cultural meaning?", "Individual / community / society", "Arnould & Thompson (2005)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: theories of consumer behavior and branding.")
```

Three organising ideas recur. First, consumers evaluate offerings against
**standards** (expectations, schemas, reference prices, the self), so the same
objective product can delight one person and disappoint another. Second, brands
are **knowledge structures** in memory that carry functional, symbolic, and
emotional meaning, and that meaning is co-authored by firms, consumers, and the
wider culture. Third, many of the most consequential effects in this chapter are
**asymmetric**: losses loom larger than gains, transgressions matter more for
some brands than others, and extensions can dilute as well as leverage. The
chapter connects to [Prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)), the
[Endowment effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect)), [Social identity
theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)), and the [Elaboration likelihood
model](#elaboration-likelihood-model) (Section \@ref(elaboration-likelihood-model)), and it prepares the ground for the
firm-level theories of the next chapter, such as [Market
orientation](#market-orientation) (Section \@ref(market-orientation)) and [Customer equity](#customer-equity) (Section \@ref(customer-equity)).

## Expectancy-Disconfirmation Theory {#expectancy-disconfirmation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Satisfaction results from comparing perceived performance with
prior expectations. Performance that exceeds expectations (positive
disconfirmation) raises satisfaction, and performance that falls short
(negative disconfirmation) lowers it, over and above the levels of expectations
and performance themselves.

**Origins.** Consumer psychology and marketing, building on adaptation-level
and assimilation-contrast ideas [@anderson1973]. Formalised by @oliver1980 and
tested against rival specifications by @churchill1982. Extended to firm-level
data by @anderson1993.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer, aggregated to firms, industries, and
national indices.

**Key constructs.** Expectations (predictive standards), perceived performance,
disconfirmation (subjective comparison), satisfaction, repurchase intention,
complaining, [word of mouth](#social-transmission) (Section \@ref(social-transmission)).

**Boundary conditions.** Expectations must exist before consumption and
performance must be evaluable. For complex durables or credence services,
performance may dominate and disconfirmation matters less. Asymmetries are
expected: shortfalls hurt more than equivalent surpluses help.

**Related theories.** [Prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)),
[Hedonic adaptation](#hedonic-adaptation) (Section \@ref(hedonic-adaptation)), [Service quality gap
model](#service-quality-gap-model) (Section \@ref(service-quality-gap-model)), [Customer equity](#customer-equity) (Section \@ref(customer-equity)),
[Cognitive dissonance theory](#cognitive-dissonance-theory) (Section \@ref(cognitive-dissonance-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Early research on consumer satisfaction borrowed two ideas from psychology. The
first was **assimilation**: consumers who expect a product to be good may
perceive it as better than it is, pulling perceptions toward expectations. The
second was **contrast**: a product that falls short may be perceived as worse
than it is because the gap is magnified. @anderson1973 set these rival
predictions against each other experimentally and helped establish disconfirmed
expectations as a central variable in satisfaction research.

@oliver1980 reorganised the field around a simple but powerful structure.
Expectations create a frame of reference. After consumption, the consumer
judges whether performance was better or worse than expected. That
**disconfirmation** judgment, together with the expectation level, determines
satisfaction, and satisfaction in turn updates attitudes and purchase
intentions. Satisfaction is therefore not a property of the product. It is a
**relative judgment** that depends on what the consumer brought to the
encounter.

### Core logic and propositions

The theory involves four constructs and two paths to satisfaction: a direct
effect of expectations (which anchor judgments) and an effect of
disconfirmation (which captures surprise relative to that anchor).

- **P1 (Disconfirmation).** Holding performance constant, satisfaction
  increases with positive disconfirmation and decreases with negative
  disconfirmation [@oliver1980].
- **P2 (Performance).** Perceived performance affects satisfaction both directly
  and through disconfirmation. For some products, the direct path dominates:
  @churchill1982 found that satisfaction with a durable product was driven
  by performance alone, whereas expectations and disconfirmation also mattered
  for a nondurable product.
- **P3 (Asymmetry).** Negative disconfirmation has a larger effect on
  satisfaction than positive disconfirmation of the same size
  [@anderson1993].
- **P4 (Evaluability).** Disconfirmation is more likely to be perceived when
  quality is easy to evaluate [@anderson1993].
- **P5 (Consequences).** Satisfaction raises repurchase intention, but the link
  between stated satisfaction and actual repurchase is nonlinear and differs
  across customer groups [@mittal2001] (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-satisfaction)).

```{r fig-cb-satisfaction, fig.cap = "Stylised expectancy-disconfirmation relationship. Each point is a simulated customer. Satisfaction rises with disconfirmation (perceived performance minus expectations), but the slope is steeper for shortfalls than for surpluses, the asymmetry reported by Anderson and Sullivan (1993). Illustrative data, not empirical estimates.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1980)
n <- 600
cust <- tibble::tibble(
  expect  = rnorm(n, 6, 1),
  perform = rnorm(n, 6, 1.3)
) |>
  mutate(disc = perform - expect,
         sat = 60 + 3 * (expect - 6) + ifelse(disc < 0, 12 * disc, 6 * disc) + rnorm(n, 0, 5),
         sat = pmin(pmax(sat, 0), 100),
         side = ifelse(disc < 0, "Negative disconfirmation", "Positive disconfirmation"))
ggplot(cust, aes(disc, sat, colour = side)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["muted"]]) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.2, y = 95, label = "Shortfalls: steep slope", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.2, y = 20, label = "Surpluses: flatter slope", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Negative disconfirmation" = pal[["orange"]],
                                 "Positive disconfirmation" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Disconfirmation (perceived performance minus expectation)",
       y = "Satisfaction (0-100)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Falling short hurts more than exceeding helps",
       caption = "Illustrative simulation (n = 600). Slope for shortfalls set at twice the slope for surpluses.")
```

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-satisfaction-mech) shows the causal structure. The
dashed edge from expectations to perceived performance represents assimilation:
high expectations can colour the experience itself. The dotted moderator
captures evaluability, which governs how much the comparison process, rather
than raw performance, drives the judgment.

```{r fig-cb-satisfaction-mech, fig.cap = "Mechanism of expectancy-disconfirmation. Expectations and perceived performance feed a subjective comparison (disconfirmation), which shapes satisfaction and downstream loyalty. Based on Oliver (1980), Churchill and Surprenant (1982), and Anderson and Sullivan (1993)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  E [label = "Expectations\\n(prior standard)", %s]
  P [label = "Perceived\\nperformance", %s]
  D [label = "Disconfirmation\\n(better or worse\\nthan expected)", %s]
  S [label = "Satisfaction", %s]
  L [label = "Repurchase, word of\\nmouth, complaints", %s]
  V [label = "Ease of evaluating\\nquality", %s]
  E -> D
  P -> D
  E -> S [style = dashed, label = " anchor"]
  P -> S [label = " direct"]
  E -> P [style = dashed, label = " assimilation"]
  D -> S -> L
  V -> D [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence and extensions

The model has been tested in hundreds of studies. A meta-analysis by
@szymanski2001 found that disconfirmation and perceived fairness (equity) are
among the strongest correlates of satisfaction, while the direct effect of
expectations is weaker and more variable. @spreng1996 argued that expectations
are not the only relevant standard: consumers also compare performance with
their **desires**, and desire congruency adds explanatory power. At the firm
level, @anderson1993 used Swedish national survey data to show that perceived
quality and disconfirmation drive satisfaction and that negative
disconfirmation weighs more heavily, an asymmetry that echoes [Loss
aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)). Satisfaction research also scaled up into national
indices: the **American Customer Satisfaction Index** (ACSI) models
satisfaction as the outcome of customer expectations, perceived quality, and
perceived value, with complaints and loyalty as consequences
[@fornell1996]. @fornell2006 reported that a portfolio of firms with high ACSI
scores outperformed the market, which suggested that satisfaction is an
under-priced intangible asset.

::: {.debate}
**Is satisfaction a comparison or a feeling?** Critics argue that the
disconfirmation paradigm is too cognitive. Satisfaction also has affective
roots: @oliver1993 showed that positive and negative affect experienced during
consumption contribute to satisfaction alongside disconfirmation and
attribute-level judgments. A second debate concerns measurement:
**inferred** disconfirmation (performance minus expectation scores) and
**perceived** disconfirmation ("better or worse than expected") are not
equivalent, and the perceived version is contaminated by the satisfaction
judgment it is supposed to explain. A third debate concerns financial
consequences. @jacobson2009 re-examined the claim that satisfaction predicts
abnormal stock returns and found the effect concentrated in a small set of
firms, mostly in computer and internet industries, which raised doubts about a
general market mispricing. The exchange is a useful reminder that
satisfaction-performance links depend on industry, time window, and model
specification.
:::

### Applications in business

Expectancy-disconfirmation gives managers two levers rather than one. Firms can
raise performance, but they can also **manage expectations**: promise what
they can reliably deliver, then exceed it. Overpromising in advertising may win
the first purchase but sets up negative disconfirmation, the costliest outcome
in the asymmetric model.

::: {.business-case}
**Customer satisfaction measurement: the ACSI.** The American Customer
Satisfaction Index, launched in 1994 at the University of Michigan, surveys
customers of companies across the US economy and estimates a structural model
in which expectations, perceived quality, and perceived value drive
satisfaction, which in turn drives complaints and loyalty [@fornell1996]. Its
design embodies the theory: it does not ask only "how satisfied are you" but
measures the standards against which satisfaction is formed. Firms use ACSI
benchmarks to compare themselves with competitors and to diagnose whether a
fall in satisfaction reflects rising expectations or declining quality. The
contrast with single-question loyalty metrics is instructive. The Net
Promoter Score asks only about likelihood to recommend [@reichheld2003], and
@keiningham2007 did not find that it outperformed the ACSI in predicting
revenue growth.
:::

Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-satisfaction-metrics) presents the approaches to measuring customer satisfaction and their relation to expectancy-disconfirmation theory.

```{r tab-cb-satisfaction-metrics}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Approach, ~`What is measured`, ~`Link to the theory`, ~`Main limitation`,
  "Inferred disconfirmation", "Separate expectation and performance ratings, difference computed", "Operationalises the comparison explicitly", "Difference scores are unreliable",
  "Perceived disconfirmation", "Direct rating: better or worse than expected", "Captures the subjective comparison", "Overlaps with the satisfaction judgment",
  "ACSI structural model", "Expectations, quality, value, satisfaction, complaints, loyalty", "Embeds satisfaction in its antecedents and consequences", "Survey cost, annual cadence",
  "Net Promoter Score", "Likelihood to recommend (0-10)", "Outcome only, no standard of comparison", "Weak diagnostic value",
  "Behavioural metrics", "Repurchase, churn, complaints, returns", "Tests the satisfaction-loyalty link", "Confounded by switching costs"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Approaches to measuring customer satisfaction and their relation to expectancy-disconfirmation theory.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: launch messaging for a meal-kit service.** A start-up
tests two launch messages. Version A promises "restaurant quality in 20
minutes". Version B promises "a good weeknight dinner in about 30 minutes".
Version A lifts trial, but customers report recipes taking 35-40 minutes.
Under expectancy-disconfirmation, Version A converts a performance that is
adequate in absolute terms into a shortfall. The theory predicts higher
first-box churn for Version A, and an A/B test that tracks second-order rates
rather than sign-ups is the appropriate check.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Holding perceived performance constant, customers exposed to
  higher-expectation advertising will report lower satisfaction.
- *H2.* The effect of negative disconfirmation on churn will be larger than the
  effect of positive disconfirmation of equal magnitude.
- *H3.* The effect of disconfirmation on satisfaction will be weaker for credence
  services (e.g., financial advice) than for search or experience goods.

**Established measures.** Oliver's satisfaction items [@oliver1980], perceived
disconfirmation scales ("much worse than expected" to "much better than
expected"), and the ACSI model and survey items [@fornell1996].

**Designs.** Experiments that manipulate expectations (advertising claims) and
performance (product quality) orthogonally. Panel surveys linking satisfaction
to observed repurchase [@mittal2001]. Firm-level panels using ACSI data with
financial outcomes [@fornell2006; @jacobson2009].

**Data sources.** ACSI firm scores, customer review text (with star ratings as
satisfaction and review content as disconfirmation cues), CRM churn data.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating satisfaction as absolute.** A satisfaction score is relative to a
standard. Comparing scores across segments, brands, or time without asking
whether expectations moved can produce wrong conclusions: a luxury hotel and a
budget motel can earn identical scores for very different performance. A
related error is to measure disconfirmation and satisfaction in the same
survey block and then report a large correlation as support for the theory.
Separate the measures in time or method, or manipulate expectations directly.
:::

## Means-End Chain Theory {#means-end-chain}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers value product attributes not for their own sake but as
means to desired consequences, which in turn serve personal values. Product
knowledge is organised as chains linking **attributes**, **consequences**, and
**values**.

**Origins.** Consumer research. @gutman1982, drawing on value theory and
categorisation research. The **laddering** interview method was systematised
by @reynolds1988. @zeithaml1988 applied the logic to price, quality, and value.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer, aggregated to segments through
hierarchical value maps.

**Key constructs.** Concrete and abstract attributes, functional and
psychosocial consequences, instrumental and terminal values, ladders,
implication matrix, hierarchical value map.

**Boundary conditions.** Most informative for involving products where
consumers can articulate reasons. Less useful for habitual, low-involvement
purchases where chains are short or absent.

**Related theories.** [Schwartz values](#schwartz-values) (Section \@ref(schwartz-values)),
[Expectancy theory](#expectancy-theory) (Section \@ref(expectancy-theory)), [Self-congruity](#self-congruity),
[Hedonic and utilitarian consumption](#hedonic-utilitarian).
:::

### Core logic

@gutman1982 proposed that consumers choose actions that produce desired
consequences and minimise undesired ones, and that values give consequences
their positive or negative valence. Product attributes matter because they are
associated, in the consumer's mind, with consequences that are themselves
linked to values. The result is a cognitive chain: *attribute* (what the product
has) leads to *consequence* (what it does for me) leads to *value* (why that
matters to me).

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-ladder) shows an illustrative ladder for a running shoe.
The same attribute can lead to different values for different consumers, which
is why means-end analysis is a segmentation tool as much as a theory of
motivation.

```{r fig-cb-ladder, fig.cap = "Illustrative means-end ladders for a running shoe. Two consumers start from the same attribute (cushioning) but reach different terminal values through different consequences. Laddering interviews elicit such chains by repeatedly asking why an element is important. Illustrative example, not interview data.", fig.height = 5}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  A1 [label = "Attribute:\\nextra cushioning", %s]
  A2 [label = "Attribute:\\nlight weight", %s]
  C1 [label = "Functional consequence:\\nfewer injuries", %s]
  C2 [label = "Functional consequence:\\nfaster times", %s]
  P1 [label = "Psychosocial consequence:\\nkeep running with friends", %s]
  P2 [label = "Psychosocial consequence:\\nfeel capable", %s]
  V1 [label = "Value:\\nbelonging", %s]
  V2 [label = "Value:\\nhealth and longevity", %s]
  V3 [label = "Value:\\naccomplishment", %s]
  A1 -> C1
  A2 -> C2
  A1 -> C2 [style = dashed]
  C1 -> P1
  C1 -> V2
  C2 -> P2
  P1 -> V1
  P2 -> V3
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_outcome, node_outcome, node_outcome), rankdir = "BT", height = 520)
```

### Laddering as method

@reynolds1988 described **laddering** as a semi-structured interview that
begins with a distinction the consumer draws between products (often elicited by
sorting or preference comparisons) and then repeatedly asks "why is that
important to you?" until the respondent reaches a value or cannot go further.
Responses are content-coded into attributes, consequences, and values. An
**implication matrix** counts how often each element leads to every other, and
a **hierarchical value map** (HVM) draws the dominant links above a cut-off.
Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-laddering) summarises the levels.

```{r tab-cb-laddering}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Level, ~Definition, ~`Typical laddering prompt`, ~`Coffee example`, ~`Marketing use`,
  "Concrete attribute", "Physical, observable feature", "What makes this one different?", "Single-origin beans", "Product specification",
  "Abstract attribute", "Subjective characterisation of features", "What does that mean for the product?", "Rich flavour", "Positioning claims",
  "Functional consequence", "Direct, tangible outcome of use", "Why is that important to you?", "Enjoyable morning ritual", "Benefit copy",
  "Psychosocial consequence", "Social or psychological outcome", "And why does that matter?", "Moment to myself before work", "Emotional appeals",
  "Instrumental value", "Preferred mode of conduct", "Why is that important to you?", "Being in control of my day", "Brand character",
  "Terminal value", "Desired end state", "And why is that important?", "Inner harmony, self-respect", "Leverage point for advertising"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Levels of a means-end chain with an illustrative coffee ladder. Example responses are hypothetical.")
```

### Evidence and critique

Means-end analysis has been used to study food, financial services, tourism,
and advertising, and it shaped how agencies translate product features into
value-based communication. @zeithaml1988 used a means-end framework to show
that consumers move from intrinsic and extrinsic cues to perceived quality,
perceived sacrifice, and perceived value, a structure still used in pricing
research.

::: {.debate}
**Are ladders discovered or constructed?** @grunert1995 questioned whether
laddering reveals stable cognitive structures or prompts respondents to
construct plausible chains on the spot. "Why" probing may push people to
higher abstraction than their actual decision process involves. Hard laddering
(questionnaire formats) and the **association pattern technique**, which asks
respondents to tick links in predefined attribute-consequence and
consequence-value matrices, offer more scalable and comparable alternatives
[@terhofstede1998]. The cost is that predefined lists can miss idiosyncratic
meanings that soft interviews reveal.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**From attribute claims to value platforms.** Many mature categories compete on
attribute parity: most toothpastes fight cavities, most cars are safe. Means-end
analysis helps brand managers find the level of the ladder where
differentiation is still possible. A car maker's safety engineering
(attribute) can lead to "protecting my family" (psychosocial consequence) and to
"being a responsible parent" (value). Volvo's long association with safety is a
familiar public example of a brand that built its positioning around one ladder
and kept it consistent across decades. The research task is to verify that the
target segment's ladder actually runs through the claimed attribute, rather
than assuming it.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Advertising that connects an attribute to a terminal value from the
  segment's dominant ladder will produce more favourable brand attitudes than
  advertising that stops at the functional consequence.
- *H2.* Ladders will be longer (reach more abstract levels) for high-involvement
  than for low-involvement categories.

**Measures and designs.** Soft laddering interviews coded into an implication
matrix and HVM [@reynolds1988]. The association pattern technique for large
samples and cross-national segmentation [@terhofstede1998]. Value inventories
such as the [Schwartz value](#schwartz-values) (Section \@ref(schwartz-values)) survey to validate the value
level.
:::

## Customer-Based Brand Equity {#customer-based-brand-equity}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** A brand has positive equity when consumers respond more
favourably to its marketing (its product, price, promotion, or distribution)
than they would to the same marketing for an unnamed or fictitious version.
That differential response arises from **brand knowledge** in memory: awareness
of the brand and the favourability, strength, and uniqueness of its
associations [@keller1993].

**Origins.** Marketing. @aaker1991 framed brand equity as a set of assets and
liabilities linked to a brand name. @keller1993 developed the
consumer-psychological account grounded in associative memory. @keller2006
review the research programme.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer (brand knowledge), aggregated to the
brand and the firm (price premiums, market share, firm value).

**Key constructs.** Brand awareness (recall, recognition), brand image, brand
associations (type, favourability, strength, uniqueness), perceived quality,
brand loyalty, differential response.

**Boundary conditions.** Equity is defined relative to a comparison (an
unbranded or fictitious product) and to a consumer segment. Associations that
are favourable in one segment or market may be neutral or negative in another.

**Related theories.** [Signaling theory](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)),
[Market-based assets](#market-based-assets) (Section \@ref(market-based-assets)), [Brand personality](#brand-personality),
[Schema congruity](#schema-congruity), [Mere exposure effect](#mere-exposure-effect) (Section \@ref(mere-exposure-effect)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Brand equity became a managerial priority in the late 1980s, when a wave of
acquisitions placed large financial values on brand names and practitioners
asked what, exactly, they were paying for. @aaker1991 answered with an asset
view: brand equity comprises **brand loyalty**, **name awareness**,
**perceived quality**, **brand associations**, and other proprietary assets
such as trademarks and channel relationships. Each adds or subtracts value for
the customer and the firm.

@keller1993 moved the definition inside the consumer's head. Building on
associative network models of memory, he defined **customer-based brand
equity** as the differential effect that brand knowledge has on how consumers
respond to the brand's marketing. Brand knowledge has two components. **Brand
awareness** is the ability to recall or recognise the brand. **Brand image** is
the set of associations linked to the brand node in memory. The definition's
power lies in its comparative structure: equity is not how much people like a
brand, but how much *more* they respond to the same marketing action because the
brand name is attached.

### Core logic and propositions

- **P1 (Awareness as a threshold).** Brand awareness is necessary for equity: a
  brand must be in the consideration set before its associations can matter.
- **P2 (Image).** Given awareness, equity increases with the **favourability**,
  **strength**, and **uniqueness** of brand associations [@keller1993].
- **P3 (Differential response).** High-equity brands enjoy higher willingness
  to pay, lower price elasticity, greater advertising and promotion
  effectiveness, and more favourable evaluations of brand extensions.
- **P4 (Credibility).** Brand investments make brand promises credible, which
  reduces perceived risk and information costs. @erdem1998 formalise this as a
  [signaling](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)) account of brand equity (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-cbbe)).

```{r fig-cb-cbbe, fig.cap = "Customer-based brand equity as a memory structure. Awareness and the characteristics of brand associations jointly produce a differential response to marketing, which appears in market and financial outcomes. Based on Keller (1993) and Keller and Lehmann (2006)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  AW [label = "Brand awareness\\n(recall, recognition)", %s]
  IM [label = "Brand image\\n(associations)", %s]
  FA [label = "Favourability", %s]
  ST [label = "Strength", %s]
  UN [label = "Uniqueness", %s]
  DR [label = "Differential response\\nto marketing", %s]
  OUT [label = "Price premium, loyalty,\\nextension success,\\nfirm value", %s]
  FA -> IM
  ST -> IM
  UN -> IM
  AW -> DR
  IM -> DR
  DR -> OUT
', node_construct, node_construct, node_moderator, node_moderator, node_moderator, node_mechanism, node_outcome))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-demand) translates P3 into a stylised demand
comparison. The branded and unbranded products are physically identical. The
branded product sells more at every price and loses fewer buyers when the price
rises: brand equity shows up as both a level shift and a flatter demand curve.

```{r fig-cb-demand, fig.cap = "Stylised differential response. The same product sold under a strong brand name and without a brand faces different demand curves: more buyers at every price and lower price sensitivity. The vertical gap at a common price corresponds to the revenue premium measure of Ailawadi, Lehmann and Neslin (2003). Illustrative curves, not estimates.", fig.height = 4}
price <- seq(2, 10, by = 0.1)
dem <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(price, units = 1000 * exp(-0.16 * (price - 2)), version = "Branded"),
  tibble::tibble(price, units = 700 * exp(-0.30 * (price - 2)), version = "Unbranded (same product)")
)
ggplot(dem, aes(price, units, colour = version)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 6, xend = 6, y = 700 * exp(-0.30 * 4), yend = 1000 * exp(-0.16 * 4),
           colour = ink[["secondary"]], arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), ends = "both")) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.2, y = 300, label = "Differential response\nat the same price", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Branded" = pal[["blue"]], "Unbranded (same product)" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  labs(x = "Price", y = "Units demanded", colour = NULL,
       title = "Brand equity as a shift and a flattening of demand",
       caption = "Stylised: branded demand = 1000 exp(-0.16 (p - 2)), unbranded = 700 exp(-0.30 (p - 2)).")
```

### Evidence and extensions

Evidence comes from three levels, summarised by @keller2006 and in Table
\@ref(tab:tab-cb-equity-levels). At the **customer-mindset** level, survey scales
measure awareness, associations, perceived quality, and loyalty
[@yoo2001]. At the **product-market** level, @ailawadi2003 proposed the
**revenue premium**, the extra revenue a brand earns relative to a private
label, as an outcome measure that is objective, comparable across brands, and
sensitive to changes in brand health. At the **financial-market** level,
researchers relate brand metrics to firm value. Brand equity also predicts the
success of brand extensions [@aaker1990; @volckner2006], a topic we return to
under [schema congruity](#schema-congruity).

```{r tab-cb-equity-levels}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Level, ~`What is measured`, ~`Example measures`, ~Strength, ~Weakness,
  "Customer mindset", "Awareness, associations, perceived quality, loyalty", "Multidimensional brand equity scale (Yoo & Donthu, 2001), association elicitation", "Diagnostic: shows why equity is high or low", "Does not directly show market value",
  "Product market", "Price and volume premium over a benchmark", "Revenue premium versus private label (Ailawadi et al., 2003), conjoint brand part-worths", "Objective, comparable, tracks change", "Needs a credible benchmark product",
  "Financial market", "Contribution of the brand to firm value", "Event studies, brand value rankings", "Speaks the language of finance", "Hard to isolate the brand from other intangibles",
  "Asset view", "Loyalty, awareness, perceived quality, associations, proprietary assets", "Aaker (1991) brand equity dimensions", "Managerially complete", "Mixes causes and outcomes"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Three levels at which brand equity is measured, plus Aaker's asset view. Organised following Keller and Lehmann (2006).")
```

::: {.debate}
**Memory, signal, or market asset?** The associative-memory account
[@keller1993] and the signaling account [@erdem1998] make overlapping
predictions but differ in mechanism. Memory accounts emphasise what consumers
know and feel about a brand. Signaling accounts emphasise that brand investments
are a bond the firm forfeits if it cheats, so equity should be greatest where
quality is hard to observe. A second critique targets measurement
proliferation: customer-mindset scales can be high while market outcomes
stagnate, and many studies validate a scale against attitudes measured in the
same survey. Linking mindset metrics to observed market behaviour remains the
field's central measurement challenge [@keller2006].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**New Coke and the location of brand equity.** Coca-Cola's 1985 reformulation
was supported by blind taste tests in which the new formula was preferred.
What the tests did not measure was the brand knowledge that consumers attached
to the original product: associations with tradition, personal memories, and
American identity. Replacing the formula threatened those associations, and
the company restored the original under the Coca-Cola Classic name within
months. In CBBE terms, the taste tests measured the response to the *unbranded*
product, while the market responded to the *branded* product. The difference
between the two is precisely what Keller's definition calls brand equity.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Private labels and the revenue premium.** Retailers' own brands compete
directly on the dimension where manufacturer brands claim superiority. Tracking
the revenue premium of a national brand over the store brand in the same
category, as @ailawadi2003 propose, gives brand managers an early warning
signal: a shrinking premium indicates eroding equity even when unit share is
stable because of promotions.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The price elasticity of demand will be lower for brands with stronger and
  more unique associations, controlling for perceived quality.
- *H2.* The positive effect of brand equity on extension evaluations will be
  stronger when perceived fit is high.
- *H3.* The effect of brand equity on choice will be larger for experience and
  credence goods than for search goods (signaling account).

**Established scales and measures.** Multidimensional brand equity scale
[@yoo2001]. Aaker's dimensions [@aaker1991]. Free association tasks coded for
favourability, strength, and uniqueness. Revenue premium from scanner data
[@ailawadi2003].

**Designs.** Branded versus unbranded (or fictitious-brand) experiments. Choice
models estimating brand intercepts and price coefficients. Panel data linking
brand-tracking surveys to sales.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Measuring equity without the "differential".** Many studies label brand
attitude, awareness, or advertising spend "brand equity". Keller's construct is
comparative: it requires a benchmark (an unbranded, fictitious, or private-label
version) and a response to marketing. Without the comparison, a study measures
liking or awareness, not equity.
:::

## Brand Personality {#brand-personality}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers ascribe human personality traits to brands. In the
United States these perceptions are organised along five dimensions:
**sincerity**, **excitement**, **competence**, **sophistication**, and
**ruggedness** [@aaker1997].

**Origins.** Consumer psychology, adapting trait psychology and the Big Five
lexical approach to brands [@aaker1997].

**Level of analysis.** The brand, as perceived by consumers.

**Key constructs.** Brand personality dimensions and facets, brand-user
imagery, self-expression.

**Boundary conditions.** The five-factor structure was derived from ratings
aggregated across brands from many categories. It does not necessarily hold for
individual brands within one category or in other cultures.

**Related theories.** [Self-congruity](#self-congruity),
[Consumer-brand relationships](#consumer-brand-relationships),
[Customer-based brand equity](#customer-based-brand-equity),
[Identity signaling](#identity-signaling) (Section \@ref(identity-signaling)).
:::

### Core logic

@aaker1997 defined **brand personality** as the set of human characteristics
associated with a brand. Personality traits can be transferred to a brand
directly, through the people associated with it (typical users, employees,
endorsers), and indirectly, through product attributes, logo, advertising style,
and price. Brand personality serves a **self-expressive** function: consumers
can use brands to express their actual or ideal selves, which links the theory
to [self-congruity](#self-congruity).

Aaker developed her scale by having a large US sample rate well-known brands
on a broad set of traits and then reducing the ratings by factor analysis.
Three of the resulting dimensions (sincerity, excitement, competence) resemble
Big Five human personality factors, while sophistication and ruggedness have no
close human counterpart and appear to capture aspirational qualities that
consumers want but do not necessarily have. Table
\@ref(tab:tab-cb-personality) lists the dimensions and their facets.

```{r tab-cb-personality}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~Facets, ~`Human personality analogue`, ~`Typical positioning`,
  "Sincerity", "Down-to-earth, honest, wholesome, cheerful", "Agreeableness", "Family, trust, care",
  "Excitement", "Daring, spirited, imaginative, up-to-date", "Extraversion", "Youth, novelty, energy",
  "Competence", "Reliable, intelligent, successful", "Conscientiousness", "Expertise, dependability",
  "Sophistication", "Upper class, charming", "No close analogue", "Luxury, refinement",
  "Ruggedness", "Outdoorsy, tough", "No close analogue", "Strength, outdoors, masculinity"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Aaker's (1997) five dimensions of brand personality and their facets.")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-personality) shows the illustrative brand personality profiles for two hypothetical brands in the same category, measured on Aaker's five dimensions (1-5 scale).

```{r fig-cb-personality, fig.cap = "Illustrative brand personality profiles for two hypothetical brands in the same category, measured on Aaker's five dimensions (1-5 scale). Profile comparisons like this guide positioning, but within-category differences may not reproduce the five-factor structure. Stylised data.", fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(1997)
prof <- tibble::tibble(
  dimension = factor(rep(c("Sincerity", "Excitement", "Competence", "Sophistication", "Ruggedness"), 2),
                     levels = rev(c("Sincerity", "Excitement", "Competence", "Sophistication", "Ruggedness"))),
  brand = rep(c("Brand A (heritage)", "Brand B (challenger)"), each = 5),
  score = c(4.3, 2.6, 4.0, 3.1, 2.4, 2.9, 4.4, 3.5, 2.7, 3.0)
)
ggplot(prof, aes(score, dimension, colour = brand)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = dimension), colour = ink[["grid"]], linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Brand A (heritage)" = pal[["blue"]], "Brand B (challenger)" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 5), breaks = 1:5) +
  labs(x = "Mean rating (1 = not at all descriptive, 5 = extremely descriptive)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "Two positioning strategies on the brand personality map",
       caption = "Stylised scores for hypothetical brands. Not empirical data.")
```

### Evidence and critique

Brand personality has been linked to brand attitudes, attachment, and loyalty,
and it moderates how consumers respond to brand transgressions: relationships
with **sincere** brands can be more fragile after a transgression than
relationships with **exciting** brands [@aaker2004], which we discuss in the
next section. @malar2011 show that a brand personality that matches the
consumer's actual self strengthens emotional attachment.

::: {.debate}
**Does the scale measure personality, and does it generalise?** Three critiques
dominate. First, @azoulay2003 argue that the scale's definition is too loose:
items such as "upper class", "intelligent", or "successful" describe social
status, competence, or user imagery rather than personality in the
psychological sense. Second, @austin2003 found that the five-factor framework
did not replicate when applied to individual brands within a single product
category, which is exactly the setting in which brand managers want to use it.
Third, the structure varies across cultures. In response, @geuens2009
developed a shorter measure restricted to personality traits that performs
better at the level of individual brands and across categories. Researchers
should choose between the scales according to the comparison they need to make.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Personifying platforms: Apple's "Get a Mac" campaign.** Between 2006 and 2009
Apple ran a long series of television spots in which two actors personified the
Mac (casual, relaxed, creative) and the PC (formal, fussy, prone to problems).
The campaign is an unusually literal application of brand personality: it
assigned excitement and sincerity to one brand and a caricature of
bureaucratic competence to its rival, and it invited viewers to choose the
character they would rather be. It also illustrates the risk of personality
positioning: a personality defined against a rival depends on consumers
accepting the caricature, and a competitor can respond by reclaiming the
traits, as Microsoft's own counter-campaign attempted.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Congruence between a brand's personality and the consumer's actual
  self will predict emotional brand attachment more strongly than congruence with
  the ideal self, especially for consumers low in self-esteem.
- *H2.* An advertising style manipulation (spontaneous versus formal) will shift
  perceived excitement but not perceived competence.

**Established scales.** Aaker's 42-item brand personality scale [@aaker1997].
The 12-item scale of @geuens2009 for within-category comparisons.

**Designs.** Repeated-measures ratings of multiple brands with multilevel
factor analysis (separating between-brand and within-respondent variance).
Experiments manipulating personality cues in advertising or packaging.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Using the scale off the shelf for within-category positioning.** Aaker's
dimensions were derived across categories. Applying them to compare three
banks or four running-shoe brands, and then interpreting each dimension as if
the structure held, invites the problem documented by @austin2003. Test the
factor structure in your own data, consider the @geuens2009 alternative, and
do not treat "competence" ratings of a bank as a statement about its
personality rather than its perceived performance.
:::

## Consumer-Brand Relationships {#consumer-brand-relationships}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers can form relationships with brands that resemble
interpersonal relationships in their forms, norms, and dynamics. The brand is
an active partner whose marketing actions are interpreted as behaviour, and
relationship quality predicts stability, forgiveness, and loyalty
[@fournier1998].

**Origins.** Consumer research. @fournier1998, using phenomenological case
studies and interpersonal relationship theory. Extended by work on relationship
norms [@aggarwal2004], transgressions [@aaker2004], emotional attachment
[@thomson2005], brand attachment [@park2010], and brand love [@batra2012].

**Level of analysis.** Dyad (consumer and brand), embedded in communities.

**Key constructs.** Relationship forms, brand relationship quality (BRQ),
relationship norms (exchange and communal), brand attachment (brand-self
connection, prominence), brand love, transgression and repair.

**Boundary conditions.** Most applicable when brands carry symbolic or emotional
meaning and are used repeatedly. For many low-involvement purchases, consumers
have habits, not relationships.

**Related theories.** [Commitment-trust theory](#commitment-trust-theory) (Section \@ref(commitment-trust-theory)),
[Social exchange theory](#social-exchange-theory) (Section \@ref(social-exchange-theory)),
[Self-congruity](#self-congruity), [Brand personality](#brand-personality).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@fournier1998 argued that the relationship metaphor is legitimate only if
brands can act as partners. Brands do act, she reasoned, because consumers
interpret marketing actions (a new advertising campaign, a price increase, a
product change) as the behaviour of a partner. Through in-depth interviews
with three women about the brands in their lives, Fournier identified a
typology of relationship forms, from arranged marriages and casual friendships
to committed partnerships, flings, dependencies, and enmities, and a model of
**brand relationship quality** with six facets: love and passion, self-connection,
interdependence, commitment, intimacy, and brand partner quality.

Later work specified the mechanisms more precisely:

- **Norms.** @aggarwal2004 showed that consumers apply interpersonal
  relationship norms to brands. In **exchange** relationships, consumers expect
  quid pro quo. In **communal** relationships, they expect care, and being
  charged for a small favour feels like a violation.
- **Transgressions.** @aaker2004 followed consumers' relationships with an
  online photo service in a longitudinal field experiment. Relationships with a
  brand given a **sincere** personality deepened over time but were damaged by a
  service transgression, while relationships with an **exciting** brand showed
  signs of reinvigoration after a transgression followed by repair.
- **Attachment.** @thomson2005 developed a scale of emotional attachment to
  brands (affection, passion, connection). @park2010 defined **brand
  attachment** as the strength of the bond connecting the brand with the self,
  reflected in brand-self connection and the prominence of brand-related
  thoughts, and showed that attachment predicts behaviours that require
  consumers to invest their own resources better than attitude strength does (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-transgression)).

```{r fig-cb-transgression, fig.cap = "Stylised relationship trajectories after a brand transgression, following the pattern reported by Aaker, Fournier and Brasel (2004). Relationship strength with a sincere brand grows faster but does not recover after a service failure, while relationship strength with an exciting brand dips and then partially rebounds after repair. Illustrative values, not study data.", fig.height = 4}
wk <- 0:10
traj <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(week = wk, strength = c(3.0, 3.4, 3.8, 4.1, 4.3, 3.4, 3.3, 3.3, 3.2, 3.2, 3.2), brand = "Sincere brand"),
  tibble::tibble(week = wk, strength = c(3.0, 3.2, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.0, 3.3, 3.6, 3.8, 3.9, 3.9), brand = "Exciting brand")
)
ggplot(traj, aes(week, strength, colour = brand)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4.5, xmax = 5.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["red"]], alpha = 0.10) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 5, y = 4.55, label = "Transgression\nand apology", size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Sincere brand" = pal[["blue"]], "Exciting brand" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = wk) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(2.5, 4.7)) +
  labs(x = "Week of relationship", y = "Relationship strength (index)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Personality shapes how relationships survive a failure",
       caption = "Stylised trajectories for illustration only.")
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-relationships) presents the selected relationship forms and constructs in consumer-brand relationship research.

```{r tab-cb-relationships}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Construct, ~Definition, ~`Illustrative consumer statement`, ~Source,
  "Committed partnership", "Long-term, voluntary, socially supported union with high love and intimacy", "I would never switch, this brand is part of how I cook", "Fournier (1998)",
  "Arranged marriage", "Non-voluntary union imposed by a third party, with little affect", "It is the detergent my partner always buys", "Fournier (1998)",
  "Fling", "Short-term, high emotional reward, no commitment", "I tried that energy drink all summer", "Fournier (1998)",
  "Enmity", "Intense negative affect and desire to avoid or harm the partner", "I tell everyone not to use that airline", "Fournier (1998)",
  "Exchange norm", "Benefits given in expectation of comparable return", "I pay, they deliver, that is the deal", "Aggarwal (2004)",
  "Communal norm", "Benefits given out of concern for the partner's needs", "They should help me without charging for it", "Aggarwal (2004)",
  "Brand attachment", "Strength of the bond between brand and self (connection, prominence)", "Thoughts about this brand come to me naturally", "Park et al. (2010)",
  "Brand love", "Passion, self-brand integration, positive emotional connection, anticipated separation distress", "I would feel anxious if this brand disappeared", "Batra et al. (2012)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Selected relationship forms and constructs in consumer-brand relationship research. Consumer statements are illustrative.")
```

### Evidence and critique

The relationship perspective has been productive: it explains why loyal
customers sometimes punish a beloved brand harshly after a betrayal, why
communal brands face backlash when they monetise previously free services
[@aggarwal2004], and why attachment predicts costly behaviours such as
recommending, defending, and paying a premium [@park2010].

::: {.debate}
**Relationship or habit?** Sceptics argue that the metaphor overreaches. Most
purchase behaviour in repeat-purchase categories follows regularities that
require no relationship construct: small brands have fewer buyers who are also
somewhat less loyal, the pattern known as **double jeopardy**
[@ehrenberg1990b]. On this view, "loyalty" is mostly a by-product of
penetration and habit, and investments in deep relationships pay off only for a
minority of customers. Relationship theorists reply that the metaphor is most
useful where it was developed, for symbolically rich brands and heavy users,
and that it predicts responses to transgressions and norm violations that
penetration models cannot. The productive position is to treat relationship
strength as a variable that is high for some consumer-brand dyads and absent
for most.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Harley-Davidson and Apple: relationship brands with communities.**
Harley-Davidson founded the Harley Owners Group (H.O.G.) in 1983, giving
owners rides, rallies, and local chapters organised around the brand. An
ethnography of new bikers by @schouten1995 described a **subculture of
consumption** whose core values (personal freedom, American heritage, and
machismo) were expressed through the motorcycle, clothing, and rituals, and
in which the company actively participated. @muniz2001 studied brand
communities around Ford Bronco, Macintosh, and Saab and identified three
markers of community: consciousness of kind, shared rituals and traditions,
and a sense of moral responsibility to other members. Apple users' defence of
the Mac against a dominant rival is a canonical example of the oppositional
loyalty that such communities sustain. The managerial lesson from both brands
is that a relationship is not only between a consumer and a brand. It is
embedded in a community that the firm can support but not fully control.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: monetising a communal brand.** A consumer electronics
brand known for friendly, free support begins charging for phone help. The
fee is modest and consistent with industry practice. Under
@aggarwal2004's norms account, customers in a communal relationship will
perceive a norm violation, and the backlash will exceed what the money
involved would predict. A better design reframes the change in exchange terms
from the outset (a premium support tier) and preserves a free communal core.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* After a service failure, customers with high brand attachment will be
  more forgiving of minor failures but more punitive after failures framed as
  betrayals of trust.
- *H2.* Charging for a previously free service will lower brand evaluations more
  under communal than under exchange relationship norms.
- *H3.* Brand attachment will predict share of wallet and advocacy better than
  brand attitude, controlling for satisfaction.

**Established scales.** Brand relationship quality facets [@fournier1998].
Emotional attachment scale [@thomson2005]. Brand attachment (connection and
prominence) [@park2010]. Brand love [@batra2012].

**Designs.** Longitudinal field experiments with manipulated brand personality
and transgressions [@aaker2004]. Relationship-norm priming experiments
[@aggarwal2004]. Phenomenological interviews and netnography for discovery.
Panel data on churn after service failures.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Assuming every customer wants a relationship.** Relationship marketing
programmes often treat all customers as potential partners. For most consumers
in most categories, brand ties are weak and choice is habitual. Segment by
relationship strength before investing in intimacy, and test whether
relationship measures add predictive power beyond satisfaction and purchase
history.
:::

## Self-Congruity Theory {#self-congruity}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers prefer products and brands whose image matches their
self-concept. The match between brand-user image and self-image
(**self-congruity**) motivates choice through the needs for self-consistency
and self-esteem [@sirgy1982]. Possessions become part of an **extended self**
[@belk1988].

**Origins.** Consumer research, drawing on self theory and symbolic
interactionism. Early statement by @grubb1967. Review and integration by
@sirgy1982. The extended self by @belk1988.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer.

**Key constructs.** Actual self, ideal self, social self, ideal social self,
brand-user image, self-congruity, self-consistency motive, self-esteem motive,
self-brand connection, extended self.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest for publicly consumed, symbolically rich
products and for consumers high in self-monitoring or public
self-consciousness. Weaker for functional, privately consumed products.

**Related theories.** [Brand personality](#brand-personality),
[Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)),
[Identity signaling](#identity-signaling) (Section \@ref(identity-signaling)),
[Psychological ownership](#psychological-ownership).
:::

### Core logic

@sirgy1982 distinguished four components of the self-concept: the **actual
self** (how I see myself), the **ideal self** (how I would like to see myself),
the **social self** (how I believe others see me), and the **ideal social
self** (how I would like others to see me). Products carry images, often
stereotypes of their typical users. When product-user image matches a
component of the self, consumption satisfies a motive: congruity with the
actual self satisfies **self-consistency**, while congruity with the ideal
self satisfies **self-esteem**. Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-selfconcept)
summarises the logic.

```{r tab-cb-selfconcept}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Self-concept component`, ~Definition, ~`Motive served by congruity`, ~`Positioning implication`,
  "Actual self", "How I see myself", "Self-consistency", "Authentic, relatable users",
  "Ideal self", "How I would like to see myself", "Self-esteem", "Aspirational users and settings",
  "Social self", "How I believe others see me", "Social consistency", "Fit with the consumer's reference group",
  "Ideal social self", "How I would like others to see me", "Social approval", "Visible, status-conferring cues"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Components of the self-concept and the motives served by self-congruity (Sirgy, 1982).")
```

@belk1988 broadened the argument: people regard their possessions as parts
of themselves. Possessions, including objects, places, people, and
collections, are incorporated into an **extended self**, for example by
controlling, creating, or coming to know them, and the involuntary loss of
possessions can feel like a loss of self. @belk2013 later extended the idea to
digital possessions, online profiles, and shared digital spaces (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-selfcongruity)).

```{r fig-cb-selfcongruity, fig.cap = "Mechanism of self-congruity. A brand-user image is compared with components of the self-concept. Actual-self congruity serves self-consistency and ideal-self congruity serves self-esteem, both feeding attachment and choice. Public consumption and self-monitoring strengthen the link. Based on Sirgy (1982) and Malar et al. (2011)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  BI [label = "Brand-user image", %s]
  AS [label = "Actual self", %s]
  IS [label = "Ideal self", %s]
  C1 [label = "Actual-self\\ncongruity", %s]
  C2 [label = "Ideal-self\\ncongruity", %s]
  M1 [label = "Self-consistency\\nmotive", %s]
  M2 [label = "Self-esteem\\nmotive", %s]
  OUT [label = "Brand attitude,\\nattachment, choice", %s]
  MOD [label = "Public consumption,\\nself-monitoring", %s]
  BI -> C1
  BI -> C2
  AS -> C1
  IS -> C2
  C1 -> M1 -> OUT
  C2 -> M2 -> OUT
  MOD -> OUT [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator), height = 380)
```

### Evidence and extensions

Self-congruity predicts brand preference, store patronage, and loyalty across
many categories. Three extensions refine it. First, @escalas2003 showed that
consumers form **self-brand connections** with brands used by groups they
belong to or aspire to join, and avoid brands associated with dissociative
groups, which links the theory to [Social identity
theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)). Second, @aaker1999 showed that the self is
malleable: the traits that drive brand preference depend on which aspects of
the self are made salient by the situation. Third, @malar2011 found that
congruity with the actual self drives emotional brand attachment more strongly
than congruity with the ideal self, with the ideal-self effect depending on
involvement, self-esteem, and public self-consciousness. Aspirational branding
is therefore not always the stronger strategy.

::: {.debate}
**How should congruity be measured?** Traditional studies rated the brand and
the self on the same list of adjectives and computed a discrepancy score.
@sirgy1997 argued that this method suffers from the unreliability of difference
scores, the use of predetermined images that may be irrelevant to the
consumer, and an implausible assumption that consumers compute congruity
attribute by attribute. They proposed a **direct** method: respondents imagine
the typical user and rate how well that image matches their own, and the direct
method showed stronger predictive validity.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Actual versus ideal self in beauty advertising.** For decades, beauty
advertising relied on ideal-self appeals: idealised models and aspirational
settings. Dove's "Campaign for Real Beauty", launched in 2004, used women of
varied ages and body types instead, an actual-self appeal. The campaign is
widely studied as a repositioning that traded the self-esteem motive for
self-consistency and authenticity. The research of @malar2011 offers one
explanation for why such a move can strengthen attachment: actual-self
congruity tends to be the more powerful driver of emotional bonds.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The effect of self-congruity on brand preference will be stronger for
  publicly consumed than for privately consumed products.
- *H2.* Actual-self congruity will predict emotional brand attachment more strongly
  than ideal-self congruity, and the difference will be larger for consumers
  low in public self-consciousness.

**Established measures.** Direct self-congruity items [@sirgy1997].
Self-brand connection scale [@escalas2003]. Brand personality ratings for the
brand and the self [@aaker1997].

**Designs.** Experiments that prime the actual or ideal self. Surveys linking
congruity to observed choice. Qualitative studies of the extended self and
possession rituals.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating congruity with similarity scores.** Computing the absolute
difference between self and brand ratings on a fixed list of traits is the
default in many studies, but it inherits the problems of difference scores and
may miss the images that actually matter to the consumer. Use direct congruity
measures or polynomial regression with response surface analysis when you need
to model fit between two separately measured profiles.
:::

## Schema Congruity Theory {#schema-congruity}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers evaluate a new product by comparing it with the
schema of the category or brand it belongs to. Products that are
**moderately incongruent** with the schema can be evaluated more favourably
than fully congruent or extremely incongruent ones, because resolving a modest
surprise is itself rewarding [@mandler1982; @meyerslevy1989].

**Origins.** Cognitive psychology [@mandler1982], brought into consumer research
by @meyerslevy1989. Applied to brand extensions by @aaker1990 and
@meyerslevy1994.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer evaluating a product, brand
extension, or advertisement.

**Key constructs.** Schema, congruity, moderate incongruity, extreme
incongruity, incongruity resolution, elaboration, perceived fit, dilution.

**Boundary conditions.** The moderate incongruity advantage requires that
consumers are motivated and able to resolve the incongruity. It weakens when
perceived risk is high [@campbell2001] and depends on prior knowledge
[@peracchio1996].

**Related theories.** [Goldilocks effect](#goldilocks-effect) (Section \@ref(goldilocks-effect)),
[Customer-based brand equity](#customer-based-brand-equity),
[Processing fluency](#processing-fluency) (Section \@ref(processing-fluency)),
[Mere exposure effect](#mere-exposure-effect) (Section \@ref(mere-exposure-effect)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@mandler1982 proposed that the value people place on an object depends partly
on how well it fits the schema they bring to it. A congruent object is
familiar and predictable, which produces mild positive affect. An object that
is moderately incongruent creates arousal and prompts cognitive work. When the
incongruity can be resolved within the existing schema, the successful
resolution is experienced as positive and evaluations rise above those for
congruent objects. Extreme incongruity cannot be resolved without changing the
schema, and the resulting frustration tends to lower evaluations.

@meyerslevy1989 tested this account with new product descriptions that
matched a category schema, departed from it moderately, or departed from it
extremely. Moderately incongruent products were evaluated most favourably and
also generated more elaborative thought, consistent with Mandler's resolution
mechanism. The general pattern, an inverted U between incongruity and
evaluation, is sketched in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-congruity). The same shape
appears in research on attention to stimuli that are neither too simple nor too
complex, the [Goldilocks effect](#goldilocks-effect) (Section \@ref(goldilocks-effect)).

```{r fig-cb-congruity, fig.cap = "Stylised schema congruity effects. With low perceived risk, evaluations peak at moderate incongruity (resolution is rewarding). With high perceived risk, consumers prefer the norm and the advantage of moderate incongruity disappears. Pattern consistent with Meyers-Levy and Tybout (1989) and Campbell and Goodstein (2001). Illustrative curves.", fig.height = 4}
x <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
cong <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(incong = x, eval = 5 + 3.5 * x - 5.5 * x^2, context = "Low perceived risk"),
  tibble::tibble(incong = x, eval = 5.1 - 0.4 * x - 2.2 * x^2, context = "High perceived risk")
)
ggplot(cong, aes(incong, eval, colour = context)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = c(0.03, 0.32, 0.97), y = 6.5,
           label = c("Congruent", "Moderately\nincongruent", "Extremely\nincongruent"),
           size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = c(0, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Low perceived risk" = pal[["blue"]], "High perceived risk" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(2, 6.8)) +
  labs(x = "Incongruity between product and category or brand schema", y = "Product evaluation",
       colour = NULL, title = "A little surprise helps, a lot of surprise hurts",
       caption = "Stylised quadratic curves for illustration only.")
```

### Brand extensions as schema congruity problems

A **brand extension** uses an established brand name to enter a new category.
The parent brand is a schema, and the extension's fit with that schema shapes
evaluations. @aaker1990 found that extensions were evaluated more favourably
when the parent brand was perceived as high quality and when the extension fit
the parent, with fit reflecting complementarity, substitutability, and the
transferability of the parent's manufacturing skills. Extensions perceived as
too easy to make were evaluated less favourably, as if consumers questioned
what the brand added. A secondary analysis of eight studies across countries
by @bottomley2001 confirmed that parent quality and fit matter in general but
that the weights vary across contexts. @volckner2006 identified fit between
the parent brand and the extension as the most important driver of extension
success, followed by marketing support, parent-brand conviction, retailer
acceptance, and parent-brand experience.

Extensions also feed back into the parent schema. @loken1993 showed that
extensions with attributes inconsistent with the family brand's beliefs can
**dilute** those beliefs, especially when the extension is seen as typical of
the brand. @meyerslevy1994 found that brand names moderately incongruent with
the extension category could produce more favourable evaluations than fully
congruent names, which extends the moderate incongruity logic to naming (Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-extensions)).

```{r tab-cb-extensions}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Brand, ~`Parent schema`, ~Extension, ~Outcome, ~`Schema congruity reading`,
  "Arm & Hammer", "Baking soda: cleaning, deodorising", "Toothpaste, deodorisers, laundry products", "Long-lived extensions", "Transfer of a core benefit makes moderate category distance resolvable",
  "Honda", "Engines, reliability", "Cars, lawn mowers, generators", "Durable multi-category brand", "Fit through shared manufacturing competence",
  "Porsche", "Performance sports cars", "Cayenne sport utility vehicle (2002)", "Commercially successful despite enthusiast criticism", "Moderate incongruity resolved by performance positioning",
  "Starbucks", "Premium coffeehouse", "Bottled Frappuccino in grocery channels (with PepsiCo)", "Durable line", "Complementary category, coffee credentials transfer",
  "Bic", "Cheap, disposable pens, lighters, razors", "Low-priced perfume (late 1980s)", "Withdrawn, widely cited failure", "Extreme incongruity: disposability clashes with the symbolism of fragrance",
  "Virgin", "Challenger, irreverent service brand", "Virgin Cola (1990s)", "Failed to win lasting share", "Attitude fit, but no capability transfer against entrenched leaders"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Brand extensions from the public record interpreted through schema congruity. Outcomes are summarised at the level of public reporting.")
```

::: {.debate}
**How robust is the moderate incongruity advantage?** The inverted U is
attractive but conditional. @peracchio1996 found that prior knowledge moderates
the effect: consumers with richer category knowledge can accommodate or
discount incongruities and may evaluate products on their attributes instead.
@campbell2001 showed that when perceived risk is high, consumers prefer
congruent products, a "preference for the norm". Brand extension findings also
travel imperfectly across cultures and product sets [@bottomley2001]. A
further measurement concern is that studies rarely verify that participants
actually resolved the incongruity, the mechanism the theory relies on. The
safer claim is that moderate incongruity *can* be an advantage when
consumers have the motivation, ability, and low risk needed to resolve it.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Brand extensions that worked and failed.** Porsche's Cayenne, launched in
2002, was a sport utility vehicle from a brand defined by sports cars. Many
enthusiasts objected, but the vehicle was engineered and marketed around
performance, which allowed consumers to resolve the incongruity within the
Porsche schema ("a sports car that happens to be an SUV"). It became one of the
brand's highest-volume models. Bic's late-1980s entry into perfume offers the
contrast. The Bic schema of cheap, functional, disposable products could not
accommodate the sensory, emotional, and status meanings of fragrance, and the
line was withdrawn. The managerial test suggested by the theory is whether a
consumer can complete the sentence "It makes sense for this brand because..."
with a reason drawn from the parent schema.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Moderately incongruent brand extensions will be evaluated more
  favourably than congruent extensions under low perceived risk, but not under
  high perceived risk.
- *H2.* The moderate incongruity advantage will be mediated by incongruity
  resolution, measured as the number of resolution-related thoughts.
- *H3.* Atypical extensions with negative performance will dilute parent-brand
  beliefs less than typical extensions with negative performance.

**Measures.** Perceived fit (complementarity, substitutability, transfer)
[@aaker1990]. Thought listing coded for elaboration and resolution
[@meyerslevy1989]. Typicality ratings. Parent-brand belief change [@loken1993].

**Designs.** Between-subjects experiments with pretested congruity levels.
Field data on extension survival [@volckner2006]. Secondary analysis across
studies [@bottomley2001].
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Confusing incongruity with novelty or quality.** An "incongruent" stimulus
often also differs in attractiveness, novelty, or information content. Without
pretests that hold quality constant and a check that resolution occurred, a
favourable evaluation of the moderately incongruent product may reflect a
better product, not the resolution mechanism.
:::

## Hedonic and Utilitarian Consumption {#hedonic-utilitarian}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Products deliver **hedonic** value (pleasure, fun, fantasy,
sensory experience) and **utilitarian** value (function, instrumentality,
practicality). The two kinds of value are evaluated differently: hedonic
consumption evokes a stronger need for justification and more guilt, which
makes choice sensitive to framing, effort, and prior virtuous acts
[@hirschman1982; @dhar2000; @okada2005; @khan2006].

**Origins.** Consumer research. @hirschman1982 and @holbrook1982 introduced the
hedonic and experiential perspective. @dhar2000 and later work brought it into
behavioural decision research.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer, product, and attribute.

**Key constructs.** Hedonic value, utilitarian value, guilt, justification,
licensing, effort, acquisition versus forfeiture, mode of payment.

**Boundary conditions.** Most products have both dimensions. Effects depend on
the salience of the hedonic dimension and on whether the decision context
calls for justification (joint evaluation, accountability).

**Related theories.** [Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)),
[Self-control](#self-control) (Section \@ref(self-control)), [[Feelings-as-information](#feelings-as-information-theory) (Section \@ref(feelings-as-information-theory))
theory](#feelings-as-information-theory) (Section \@ref(feelings-as-information-theory)),
[Warm-glow heuristic](#warm-glow-heuristic) (Section \@ref(warm-glow-heuristic)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@hirschman1982 defined **hedonic consumption** as the facets of consumer
behaviour that relate to the multisensory, fantasy, and emotive aspects of
product experience. Together with @holbrook1982, who described an
experiential view of consumption built on "fantasies, feelings, and fun", they
challenged the information-processing paradigm that treated consumers as
problem solvers choosing among attribute bundles. Behavioural decision
researchers later asked how the two kinds of value trade off in choice.

Four propositions summarise the core findings:

- **P1 (Loss aversion differs).** Hedonic attributes loom larger when consumers
  give something up than when they acquire it. @dhar2000 found that consumers
  were relatively more likely to choose a hedonic item in a forfeiture decision
  (which item to give up) than in an acquisition decision (which item to get).
- **P2 (Justification).** Hedonic options are harder to justify. @okada2005
  showed that a hedonic option tends to be rated more highly when evaluated on
  its own, while a utilitarian option is more often chosen when the two are
  compared side by side, and that consumers prefer to pay for hedonic goods
  with time and for utilitarian goods with money.
- **P3 (Licensing).** A prior virtuous act, or even the intention to act
  virtuously, boosts the self-concept and licenses a subsequent hedonic choice
  [@khan2006].
- **P4 (Earned indulgence).** Effort provides a justification. @kivetz2002
  found that requiring more effort in a frequency programme shifted preferences
  toward luxury rather than necessity rewards (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-hedonic)).

```{r fig-cb-hedonic, fig.cap = "Justification mechanism in hedonic consumption. Hedonic options evoke anticipated guilt and a need for justification. Justification cues (effort, prior virtue, a charitable tie-in, evaluating the option on its own) relieve that need and increase hedonic choice. Based on Okada (2005), Khan and Dhar (2006), Kivetz and Simonson (2002), and Strahilevitz and Myers (1998)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  H [label = "Hedonic option\\n(pleasure, indulgence)", %s]
  G [label = "Anticipated guilt,\\nneed for justification", %s]
  C [label = "Choice of the\\nhedonic option", %s]
  J1 [label = "Effort earned\\n(loyalty points)", %s]
  J2 [label = "Prior virtuous act\\n(licensing)", %s]
  J3 [label = "Charity tie-in", %s]
  J4 [label = "Single rather than\\njoint evaluation", %s]
  H -> G
  G -> C [label = " inhibits", style = dashed]
  J1 -> G [label = " relieves", arrowhead = tee]
  J2 -> G [arrowhead = tee]
  J3 -> G [arrowhead = tee]
  J4 -> G [arrowhead = tee]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator, node_moderator, node_moderator, node_moderator),
  rankdir = "LR", height = 360)
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-hedonic) presents the how hedonic and utilitarian value differ in consumer decision making.

```{r tab-cb-hedonic}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~Hedonic, ~Utilitarian, ~`Key evidence`,
  "Nature of benefit", "Pleasure, fantasy, sensory and emotional experience", "Function, problem solving, instrumentality", "Hirschman & Holbrook (1982)",
  "Need for justification", "High: evokes guilt", "Low: easy to justify", "Okada (2005)",
