  "Acquisition versus forfeiture", "Weighs more when giving up", "Weighs relatively more when acquiring", "Dhar & Wertenbroch (2000)",
  "Preferred payment", "Time", "Money", "Okada (2005)",
  "Effect of a prior virtuous act", "Licensed: choice share rises", "Little change", "Khan & Dhar (2006)",
  "Effect of required effort", "Effort justifies luxury rewards", "Necessity rewards preferred at low effort", "Kivetz & Simonson (2002)",
  "Charity incentive effectiveness", "More effective", "Less effective", "Strahilevitz & Myers (1998)",
  "Measurement", "HED subscale", "UT subscale", "Voss et al. (2003)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "How hedonic and utilitarian value differ in consumer decision making.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The distinction is now standard in consumer research and is reviewed by
@alba2013. @strahilevitz1998 showed that charity incentives (a donation tied to
purchase) are more effective for frivolous products than for practical ones,
consistent with the idea that the donation offsets guilt. The two dimensions
can be measured with the HED/UT scale of @voss2003, which treats them as
separate attitude components rather than poles of a single continuum, and
shopping itself can deliver hedonic and utilitarian value [@babin1994].

::: {.debate}
**Category or dimension?** Much research classifies products as hedonic
(chocolate, concerts) or utilitarian (detergent, printer cartridges). Critics
note that the same product can be bought for either reason and that the
hedonic-utilitarian distinction overlaps with other contrasts, such as vice
versus virtue, wants versus shoulds, and luxuries versus necessities, which
have different theoretical mechanisms (self-control, status, price). Studies
that manipulate the salient goal of a purchase, or measure both dimensions
with validated scales, yield cleaner inferences than studies that rely on
category labels.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Hedonic purchase framing and loyalty programme design.** The justification
mechanism suggests several practical levers. **Effort framing**: points that
consumers feel they have earned are more likely to be spent on indulgences,
which supports offering luxury rewards (spa days, upgrades) in programmes that
require sustained effort [@kivetz2002]. **Progress framing**: loyalty cards
that present progress as already under way increase completion
[@nunes2006]. **Programme mechanics**: Starbucks moved its Rewards programme in
2016 from earning per transaction to earning per dollar spent, a change that
altered what customers had to do to earn a treat and illustrates how programme
rules shape the effort-reward link. **Cause tie-ins**: the (PRODUCT)RED
initiative, launched in 2006, partnered with brands such as Apple and Gap to
contribute part of the proceeds from special-edition products to the Global
Fund, pairing discretionary consumer products with a charitable justification,
consistent with @strahilevitz1998.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: framing a premium headphone.** A retailer tests two
product pages for premium noise-cancelling headphones. Page A emphasises sound
quality and immersive listening (hedonic). Page B adds a utilitarian frame:
"focus at work, fewer distractions on your commute". The theory predicts that
Page B lowers the need for justification and raises conversion among buyers
who would otherwise feel guilty, while Page A performs better among buyers
shopping for a gift, where justification concerns are weaker.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Requiring effort to earn a reward will increase the share of hedonic
  rewards chosen, and the effect will be mediated by reduced anticipated guilt.
- *H2.* A charitable tie-in will raise purchase likelihood more for products
  rated high on the HED subscale than for products rated high on the UT
  subscale.
- *H3.* Joint display of a hedonic and a utilitarian option will reduce the
  hedonic choice share relative to sequential display.

**Established scales.** HED/UT scale [@voss2003]. Hedonic and utilitarian
shopping value [@babin1994].

**Designs.** Choice experiments manipulating effort, prior virtue, and
evaluation mode. Field experiments in loyalty programmes. Panel data on
redemption choices.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Labelling categories instead of measuring value.** Classifying a product as
"hedonic" because it is chocolate, or "utilitarian" because it is a laptop,
ignores that consumers buy laptops for gaming and chocolate as a gift. Measure
the hedonic and utilitarian dimensions for the target consumers, and separate
the hedonic-utilitarian contrast from vice-virtue and luxury-necessity
contrasts when theorising mechanism.
:::

## Psychological Ownership {#psychological-ownership}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** People can feel that a target (an object, an idea, a brand, an
organisation) is "theirs" without legal title. This feeling of
**psychological ownership** arises from control, intimate knowledge, and
investment of the self, and it raises valuation, attachment, and
responsibility for the target [@pierce2001].

**Origins.** Organisational behaviour [@pierce2001; @pierce2003], extended to
consumers by research on touch [@peck2009], the endowment effect
[@shu2011; @reb2007], and consumer empowerment [@fuchs2010].

**Level of analysis.** Individual (with collective variants).

**Key constructs.** Feelings of ownership, routes (control, intimate knowledge,
investment of self), motives (efficacy, self-identity, having a place),
valuation, territoriality.

**Boundary conditions.** Requires a target that can be controlled, known, or
invested in. Effects can turn negative, as territoriality, when ownership
feels threatened.

**Related theories.** [Endowment effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect)),
[IKEA effect](#ikea-effect) (Section \@ref(ikea-effect)), [Self-congruity](#self-congruity),
[Self-determination theory](#self-determination-theory) (Section \@ref(self-determination-theory)).
:::

### Core logic

@pierce2001 defined psychological ownership as the state in which individuals
feel as though the target of ownership, or a piece of it, is theirs. They
proposed that the state serves three motives: **efficacy and effectance**
(being in control), **self-identity** (expressing and maintaining the self),
and **having a place** (a home or territory). Three routes produce it:
**controlling** the target, **coming to know it intimately**, and **investing
the self** in it through effort, time, or creativity. Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-cb-ownership) shows the mechanism and its consumer outcomes.

```{r fig-cb-ownership, fig.cap = "Routes to psychological ownership and their consumer outcomes. Touch, customisation, co-creation, and use produce feelings of ownership through control, intimate knowledge, and self-investment. Based on Pierce, Kostova and Dirks (2001) and Peck and Shu (2009)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  T1 [label = "Touch, trial,\\nuse", %s]
  T2 [label = "Customisation,\\nco-creation", %s]
  R1 [label = "Control", %s]
  R2 [label = "Intimate\\nknowledge", %s]
  R3 [label = "Investment\\nof self", %s]
  PO [label = "Psychological\\nownership\\n(this is mine)", %s]
  OUT [label = "Higher valuation,\\nwillingness to pay,\\nword of mouth", %s]
  M [label = "Motives: efficacy,\\nself-identity,\\nhaving a place", %s]
  T1 -> R1
  T1 -> R2
  T2 -> R1
  T2 -> R3
  R1 -> PO
  R2 -> PO
  R3 -> PO
  PO -> OUT
  M -> PO [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

### Evidence

@peck2009 showed that merely touching an object increases perceived ownership
and valuation, and that vivid imagery of touching can substitute for touch when
physical contact is not possible. @reb2007 separated legal ownership from
physical possession and found that feelings of ownership tracked valuations,
which places psychological ownership at the heart of the [Endowment
effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect)). @shu2011 showed that psychological ownership and
the affective reactions it produces help explain the size of the endowment
effect. Investment of the self is the mechanism behind the [IKEA
effect](#ikea-effect) (Section \@ref(ikea-effect)): people value products they have assembled themselves
more highly [@norton2012]. @fuchs2010 found that consumers empowered to select
which products a firm should produce showed stronger demand for those products,
with psychological ownership mediating the effect. @jussila2015 review the
marketing literature, and @morewedge2021 argue that the shift from owning to
accessing (streaming, renting, sharing) reduces the routes to psychological
ownership, with consequences for how much consumers value and care for what
they use.

::: {.business-case}
**Designing for "mine".** Retailers and brands use each route. **Touch and
trial**: open displays, in-store demonstrations, test drives, and generous
home-trial periods let consumers control and get to know a product before
purchase [@peck2009]. **Customisation**: configurators such as Nike's
online customisation service let buyers invest the self in a product's design.
**Co-creation**: LEGO Ideas invites fans to submit and vote on set designs,
giving participants a stake in products they did not legally own,
consistent with @fuchs2010. The theory also warns of a cost: customers with strong feelings
of ownership can react territorially when a firm changes "their" product or
community, as many brand-community backlashes show.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Allowing consumers to customise a product will raise willingness to pay,
  mediated by psychological ownership.
- *H2.* The effect of touch on valuation will be stronger for products with
  positive than with neutral sensory properties.
- *H3.* Access-based consumers (subscribers) will report lower psychological
  ownership and take less care of products than owners.

**Measures.** Psychological ownership items adapted from @vandyne2004 ("I feel
this is my product"). Willingness to pay and willingness to accept.

**Designs.** Touch versus no-touch experiments [@peck2009]. Empowerment
manipulations [@fuchs2010]. Field experiments with trial periods.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating psychological ownership with legal ownership or liking.** The
construct is a feeling of possession, distinct from legal title and from
attitude. Studies that infer it from ownership status or brand liking cannot
test the theory. Measure the feeling directly and show that it mediates the
outcome.
:::

## Variety Seeking {#variety-seeking}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers sometimes switch away from a familiar or preferred
option not because of a better offer but because variety itself has value, or
because they misforecast how much variety they will want [@mcalister1982;
@simonson1990].

**Origins.** Consumer research and economics of choice. Typology by
@mcalister1982. Diversification bias by @simonson1990 and @read1995.
Choosing less-preferred options for variety by @ratner1999.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer, product category.

**Key constructs.** Derived versus direct variety, satiation, stimulation
seeking, optimum stimulation level, diversification bias, sensory-specific
satiety.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest for hedonic, sensory, and frequently
purchased categories, for simultaneous choices made for future consumption,
and for consumers with a high optimum stimulation level.

**Related theories.** [Hedonic adaptation](#hedonic-adaptation) (Section \@ref(hedonic-adaptation)),
[Coolidge effect](#coolidge-effect) (Section \@ref(coolidge-effect)), [Choice architecture](#choice-architecture) (Section \@ref(choice-architecture)),
[Hedonic and utilitarian consumption](#hedonic-utilitarian).
:::

### Core logic

@mcalister1982 distinguished **derived** varied behaviour, which results from
external forces (several household members, changing situations, price
promotions, new products), from **direct** variety seeking, in which variety
itself is the goal. Direct variety seeking can be intrapersonal (satiation with
an attribute, the desire for stimulation) or interpersonal (affiliation with or
distinction from others). Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-variety) summarises the
typology.

```{r tab-cb-variety}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Type, ~Driver, ~Example, ~`Managerial implication`,
  "Derived: multiple needs", "Different users or uses in a household", "One yoghurt for children, another for adults", "Not true variety seeking: target uses",
  "Derived: changing constraints", "Promotions, stockouts, new products", "Switching to whichever brand is on deal", "Switching reflects price, not taste",
  "Direct: intrapersonal", "Satiation with attributes, stimulation seeking", "Rotating snack flavours", "Offer flavour or format variety within the brand",
  "Direct: interpersonal", "Affiliation with or distinction from others", "Trying what friends drink, or avoiding it", "Link to identity signaling and social influence"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Typology of varied behaviour following McAlister and Pessemier (1982).")
```

Variety seeking is not always a stable preference. @simonson1990 showed that
consumers who choose several items at once for future consumption choose more
variety than those who choose one item at a time, a pattern @read1995 called
**diversification bias** and demonstrated even among children choosing
Halloween candy. @ratner1999 found that people choose less-preferred songs for
the sake of variety, even though doing so lowers their enjoyment during
consumption. At the attribute level, @inman2001 showed that variety seeking
follows **sensory-specific satiety**: consumers switch flavours more than
brands. Individual differences matter as well: consumers with a high
**optimum stimulation level** engage in more exploratory behaviour, including
variety seeking [@raju1980; @steenkamp1992], and category characteristics
shape how much true variety seeking occurs [@vantrijp1996] (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-variety)).

```{r fig-cb-variety, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of diversification bias. Simulated consumers choose four snacks from six flavours either simultaneously (all at once, for the next four weeks) or sequentially (one each week). Simultaneous choosers spread choices across more distinct flavours, the pattern reported by Simonson (1990) and Read and Loewenstein (1995). Stylised parameters.", fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(1990)
pref <- c(0.40, 0.22, 0.14, 0.10, 0.08, 0.06)
sim_distinct <- function(n, mode) {
  vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    if (mode == "Sequential (one per week)") {
      length(unique(sample(1:6, 4, replace = TRUE, prob = pref)))
    } else {
      p_div <- (pref + 0.35) / sum(pref + 0.35)   # anticipated satiation flattens choice
      length(unique(sample(1:6, 4, replace = TRUE, prob = p_div)))
    }
  }, numeric(1))
}
div <- bind_rows(lapply(c("Sequential (one per week)", "Simultaneous (all at once)"), function(m)
  tibble::tibble(mode = m, distinct = sim_distinct(2000, m)))) |>
  count(mode, distinct) |>
  group_by(mode) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
ggplot(div, aes(factor(distinct), share, fill = mode)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Sequential (one per week)" = pal[["blue"]], "Simultaneous (all at once)" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Number of distinct flavours among four choices", y = "Share of consumers", fill = NULL,
       title = "Choosing in advance produces more variety",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (2,000 consumers per condition). Not empirical data.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: subscription boxes and flavour rotation.** A snack
subscription asks customers to choose a month of snacks at once. Diversification
bias predicts that they will pick more variety than they will enjoy, which can
raise later dissatisfaction with less-preferred items. Two design responses
follow from the theory: allow week-by-week swaps (converting simultaneous into
sequential choice), or default the box to a mix weighted toward each customer's
revealed favourites. Snack and beverage brands also exploit genuine
sensory-specific satiety with rotating limited-edition flavours that keep
variety seekers inside the brand rather than switching to a competitor.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses and designs.** *H1.* Bundled, advance purchases will
contain more distinct items than repeated single purchases by the same
consumers. *H2.* Brand switching driven by satiation will occur more at the
flavour than at the brand level [@inman2001]. Use scanner panels to separate
true variety seeking from promotion-driven switching, choice experiments
contrasting simultaneous and sequential choice [@simonson1990], and optimum
stimulation level scales [@raju1980; @steenkamp1992].
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Calling every switch variety seeking.** Brand switching in panel data often
reflects promotions, stockouts, or multiple household users, which
@mcalister1982 classify as derived varied behaviour. Control for price and
availability before attributing switching to a taste for variety.
:::

## Reference Price Theory {#reference-price}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers judge a price against a **reference price**, an
internal standard formed from past prices or an external standard supplied by
the environment. Prices below the reference are coded as gains and prices
above it as losses, and losses affect choice more strongly than equivalent
gains [@winer1986; @kalyanaram1995; @mazumdar2005].

**Origins.** Behavioural pricing and marketing science, drawing on
adaptation-level theory, [Prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory))
[@kahneman1979], and transaction utility in [Mental
accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)) [@thaler1985]. Brand choice models by
@winer1986. Reviews by @kalyanaram1995 and @mazumdar2005.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer, aggregated to brand demand and
retail pricing policy.

**Key constructs.** Internal reference price, external reference price,
price expectation, gain and loss, loss aversion, transaction utility,
promotion frequency.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest for frequently purchased goods with salient
price histories and for consumers who track prices. Reference effects are
harder to identify when consumers differ widely in price sensitivity
[@bell2000].

**Related theories.** [Prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)),
[Loss aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)), [Anchoring effect](#anchoring-effect) (Section \@ref(anchoring-effect)),
[Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)), [Decoy effect](#decoy-effect) (Section \@ref(decoy-effect)).
:::

### Core logic and propositions

Classical demand theory predicts that consumers respond to the current price.
Reference price theory adds that they respond to the current price *relative to
a standard*. @winer1986 built this idea into a brand choice model for
frequently purchased products, in which the reference price is a consumer's
expectation formed from the brand's past prices, and choice depends on both
the observed price and its deviation from the reference. @mayhew1992 showed
with scanner data that both **internal** (memory-based) and **external**
(point-of-purchase) reference prices affect choice.

- **P1 (Reference dependence).** Holding price constant, purchase probability
  rises when price is below the reference price and falls when it is above
  [@winer1986; @kalyanaram1995].
- **P2 (Adaptive formation).** Internal reference prices are formed largely from
  the brand's own past prices. @briesch1997 compared alternative specifications
  and found that models based on the brand's past prices fit best.
- **P3 (Asymmetry).** Consumers react more to prices above the reference (losses)
  than to prices below it (gains) [@hardie1993; @kalyanaram1995], an
  application of [Loss aversion](#loss-aversion) (Section \@ref(loss-aversion)).
- **P4 (External anchors).** Advertised regular or "compare at" prices raise
  perceived value and lower search, even when the reference is exaggerated
  [@urbany1988; @grewal1998].
- **P5 (Promotion erosion).** Because reference prices adapt, frequent
  promotions lower the internal reference price, so that the regular price
  later feels like a loss.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-cb-refprice) illustrates P5 with an adaptive reference
price. Under frequent promotions, the reference price drifts toward the deal
price, and every return to the regular price becomes a perceived loss.

```{r fig-cb-refprice, fig.cap = "Illustrative adaptive reference prices under two promotion policies. The reference price is an exponentially weighted average of past prices. Frequent promotions pull the reference price toward the deal price, so the regular price is increasingly coded as a loss. Stylised simulation.", fig.height = 4.4}
weeks <- 1:52
make_rp <- function(promo_every, label) {
  price <- ifelse(weeks %% promo_every == 0, 3, 4)
  rp <- numeric(length(weeks)); rp[1] <- 4
  for (t in 2:length(weeks)) rp[t] <- 0.75 * rp[t - 1] + 0.25 * price[t - 1]
  tibble::tibble(week = weeks, `Shelf price` = price, `Reference price` = rp, policy = label)
}
rp <- bind_rows(make_rp(8, "Occasional promotions (every 8th week)"),
                make_rp(2, "Frequent promotions (every 2nd week)")) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Shelf price`, `Reference price`), names_to = "series", values_to = "value")
ggplot(rp, aes(week, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_step(data = filter(rp, series == "Shelf price"), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = filter(rp, series == "Reference price"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~policy, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Shelf price" = ink[["muted"]], "Reference price" = pal[["blue"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar, limits = c(2.8, 4.1), breaks = c(3, 3.5, 4)) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Price", colour = NULL,
       title = "Frequent deals teach consumers a lower price",
       caption = "Stylised: regular price $4, deal price $3, reference = 0.75 x previous reference + 0.25 x previous price.")
```

Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-refprice) presents the internal and external reference prices (organised following Mazumdar, Raj, and Sinha, 2005).

```{r tab-cb-refprice}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Internal reference price`, ~`External reference price`,
  "Definition", "A price standard held in memory", "A price standard presented in the purchase environment",
  "Typical sources", "Past prices paid or seen, expected price, perceived fair price", "Advertised regular price, 'compare at' price, competitor prices, price of adjacent items",
  "Formation", "Adaptive, updated by recent prices", "Supplied by the seller or context at the point of purchase",
  "Typical measures", "Exponentially smoothed past prices, stated expected price", "Experimental manipulation of advertised reference prices",
  "Managerial lever", "Promotion depth and frequency, price consistency", "Price-comparison advertising, assortment and display",
  "Regulatory concern", "Low", "High: fictitious former prices can be deceptive",
  "Key sources", "Winer (1986), Briesch et al. (1997)", "Urbany et al. (1988), Grewal et al. (1998)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Internal and external reference prices (organised following Mazumdar, Raj, and Sinha, 2005).")
```

### Evidence and critique

@kalyanaram1995 summarised a set of empirical generalisations: reference prices
affect brand choice, past prices are a central input to their formation, and
the response to price losses is larger than the response to gains.
@mazumdar2005 organise the literature around how reference prices are formed,
how they are retrieved, and how they affect evaluations and choice, and they
offer propositions for future research.

::: {.debate}
**Is loss aversion in scanner data real?** @bell2000 showed that heterogeneity
in price sensitivity can masquerade as loss aversion. Price-sensitive
households tend to buy when prices are low (gains) and price-insensitive
households when prices are high (losses), so a pooled model can find
asymmetric responses even when no individual is loss averse. Once heterogeneity
was accounted for, estimated loss aversion shrank substantially. The debate
does not overturn reference dependence, but it means that asymmetry estimates
from aggregate data require careful modelling of consumer heterogeneity. A
second debate concerns which standard consumers actually use: the brand's own
past prices, the category's prices, or the external price at the shelf
[@briesch1997; @mayhew1992].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Outlet stores and "compare at" prices.** Outlet malls allow manufacturers to
segment price-sensitive shoppers who will travel and accept less service from
consumers who buy at full-price stores [@coughlan2005]. Price tags in outlets
often display a "compare at" or "original" price alongside the selling price.
Reference price theory explains why: an external reference raises perceived
transaction value even when consumers discount it [@urbany1988; @grewal1998].
The same mechanism creates regulatory risk. The US Federal Trade Commission's
guides against deceptive pricing address former-price comparisons, and in 2014
several members of the US Congress asked the Commission to examine whether
outlet pricing and labelling misled shoppers, partly because some outlet goods
are made specifically for outlets and were never sold at the reference price.
For managers, the lesson is that reference prices create value only while they
remain credible.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**JCPenney's "Fair and Square" pricing.** In 2012 the US department store
chain JCPenney, under a new chief executive, replaced most of its frequent
sales and coupons with simpler everyday prices. The strategy assumed that
shoppers disliked the promotional game. Sales and store traffic fell steeply,
the chief executive was replaced in 2013, and promotions returned. Reference
price theory and transaction utility [@thaler1985] suggest why: years of
promotions had taught customers low internal reference prices and a habit of
enjoying the "deal". Removing external reference prices eliminated the
perceived gain without lowering the price consumers expected to pay.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The effect of a price increase on brand choice will be larger than the
  effect of an equivalent price decrease, after controlling for household
  heterogeneity in price sensitivity.
- *H2.* Increasing promotion frequency will lower consumers' stated expected
  price for the brand.
- *H3.* Plausible external reference prices will raise perceived transaction
  value more than implausible ones, and the effect will be weaker among
  consumers with high price knowledge.

**Measures.** Internal reference price from exponentially smoothed past prices
[@winer1986; @briesch1997]. Stated expected and fair prices. Acquisition and
transaction value scales [@grewal1998].

**Designs.** Brand choice models with reference price terms estimated on
scanner panels, with latent-class or random-coefficient heterogeneity
[@bell2000]. Experiments manipulating advertised reference prices
[@urbany1988]. Field experiments varying promotion schedules.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Estimating loss aversion from pooled data.** Asymmetric price responses in
aggregate data can arise from heterogeneity, endogenous purchase timing, and
stockpiling rather than loss aversion. Model heterogeneity, account for
purchase timing, and treat asymmetry as a hypothesis to be tested rather than
a parameter to be assumed.
:::

## Consumer Culture Theory {#consumer-culture-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumption is a cultural practice. Consumers use goods,
brands, and services to construct identities, form communities, and negotiate
social structures and ideologies, and the meanings of goods are produced and
circulated by culture, firms, and consumers together [@arnould2005].

**Origins.** Interpretive consumer research drawing on anthropology, sociology,
and cultural studies [@mccracken1986; @belk1989; @holt2002]. The label
"consumer culture theory" was introduced by @arnould2005 to name a family of
perspectives rather than a single theory.

**Level of analysis.** Individual, community, market, and society.

**Key constructs.** Cultural meaning, meaning transfer, consumption rituals,
identity projects, marketplace cultures and subcultures, brand communities,
cultural capital, marketplace ideologies, authenticity.

**Boundary conditions.** Best suited to explaining meaning, identity, and
practice. It aims at theoretical transferability across contexts rather than
statistical generalisation, and it is less suited to predicting the size of
effects.

**Related theories.** [Self-congruity](#self-congruity),
[Consumer-brand relationships](#consumer-brand-relationships),
[Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)),
[Institutional theory](#institutional-theory) (Section \@ref(institutional-theory)),
[Identity signaling](#identity-signaling) (Section \@ref(identity-signaling)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@mccracken1986 offered the foundational account of how goods acquire meaning.
Cultural meaning resides first in the **culturally constituted world**, the
categories and principles through which a society organises experience. Two
institutions, **advertising** and the **fashion system**, transfer that meaning
into consumer goods. Consumers then draw meaning from goods into their own
lives through **rituals**: possession, exchange (such as gift giving), grooming,
and divestment. @mccracken1989 applied the same logic to celebrity
endorsement: celebrities carry meanings from their roles, which advertising
transfers to products and consumption transfers to consumers. Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-cb-meaning) shows the model.

```{r fig-cb-meaning, fig.cap = "McCracken's (1986) model of the movement of cultural meaning. Meaning moves from the culturally constituted world into goods through advertising and the fashion system, and from goods into consumers' lives through possession, exchange, grooming, and divestment rituals."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  W [label = "Culturally\\nconstituted world", %s]
  AF [label = "Advertising and\\nfashion system", %s]
  G [label = "Consumer goods\\nand brands", %s]
  R [label = "Consumption rituals\\n(possession, exchange,\\ngrooming, divestment)", %s]
  C [label = "Individual\\nconsumer", %s]
  W -> AF -> G -> R -> C
  C -> W [style = dashed, constraint = false, label = " consumers reshape\\n cultural meaning"]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome), height = 300)
```

@arnould2005 reviewed two decades of interpretive research and organised it
into four research programmes (Table \@ref(tab:tab-cb-cct)). The common
thread is that consumers are not merely choosers among attribute bundles but
active producers of meaning who work with, and sometimes against, the meanings
that marketers offer. @holt2002 developed this point into a dialectical theory
of branding: consumers increasingly resist brands they perceive as cultural
engineering, and brands retain value when they serve as authentic cultural
resources for consumers' own identity projects. In later work, @holt2004
argued that iconic brands succeed by offering myths that address
contradictions in a society's culture at particular historical moments.

```{r tab-cb-cct}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Research programme`, ~`Central question`, ~`Illustrative study`, ~`Managerial relevance`,
  "Consumer identity projects", "How do consumers use market resources to construct coherent selves?", "Extended self (Belk, 1988)", "Positioning brands as identity resources",
  "Marketplace cultures", "How do consumers forge communities and subcultures around consumption?", "Harley-Davidson bikers (Schouten & McAlexander, 1995), brand communities (Muniz & O'Guinn, 2001)", "Community management, co-creation",
  "Sociohistoric patterning of consumption", "How do class, gender, ethnicity, and institutions structure consumption?", "Cultural capital and taste (Holt, 1998)", "Segmentation beyond demographics",
  "Mass-mediated marketplace ideologies", "How do consumers interpret, adopt, or resist commercial meanings?", "Doppelganger brand images (Thompson et al., 2006)", "Monitoring brand meaning and backlash"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The four research programmes of consumer culture theory identified by Arnould and Thompson (2005).")
```

### Evidence and critique

CCT research has produced influential concepts: the **sacred and profane** in
consumption [@belk1989], **subcultures of consumption** [@schouten1995],
**brand communities** [@muniz2001], the structuring role of **cultural
capital** in taste [@holt1998], and the **doppelganger brand image**, a
parody of a brand's image circulated by critics that signals when emotional
branding has lost authenticity [@thompson2006]. Methodologically, it
introduced ethnography, phenomenological interviewing, and **netnography**, the
ethnographic study of online communities [@kozinets2002], into marketing.

::: {.debate}
**Theory or label, and how much context?** Sceptics from the positivist
tradition question whether findings from small, purposive samples generalise,
and whether a "family of perspectives" is a theory at all. Defenders respond
that CCT seeks analytic rather than statistical generalisation and that its
concepts have proved transferable across markets. A critique from within the
tradition is equally pointed. @askegaard2011 argue that CCT has focused too
heavily on individual consumers' lived experience and needs to attend to the
"context of context": the social, historical, and institutional structures that
shape what consumers can experience in the first place.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Meaning transfer in celebrity endorsement and cultural branding.** Nike's Air
Jordan line, launched in 1985 around a then-rookie basketball player, is a
textbook case of McCracken's meaning transfer: the athlete's cultural meanings
(excellence, style, defiance) moved into the product through advertising and
into consumers' lives through use, collecting, and display [@mccracken1989].
CCT also explains the limits of such strategies. When consumers perceive a
brand's meanings as manufactured, they produce counter-meanings, the
doppelganger images that @thompson2006 identified around Starbucks. The
managerial implication is to monitor not only what the brand says but also
what consumers and critics are saying about it, and to ground brand meaning in
practices consumers can recognise as authentic [@holt2002].
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Typical research questions and propositions.** CCT studies usually build
theory rather than test hypotheses, but they generate propositions that other
methods can test, for example: *P1.* Brand communities that share rituals and
a sense of moral responsibility will show greater resistance to competitor
switching than communities based only on product use. *P2.* Consumers with high
cultural capital will favour brands whose meanings are subtle and require
interpretive knowledge.

**Designs and data.** Ethnography and participant observation
[@schouten1995]. Phenomenological interviews. Netnography of online communities
[@kozinets2002]. Historical and archival analysis of advertising and media.
Mixed methods that pair interpretive discovery with survey or experimental
tests.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Using interpretive research as decoration.** A handful of quotations does not
make a CCT study. The tradition's contribution comes from sustained engagement
with a context, theoretically motivated sampling, and an explicit account of
how meanings are produced and contested. Conversely, quantitative researchers
should not dismiss CCT findings for lacking statistical generalisation: they
are best treated as theoretical mechanisms to be tested and bounded.
:::

## Chapter Summary {#consumer-behavior-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- Satisfaction is a **relative judgment**. Expectations, performance, and their
  comparison all matter, and shortfalls hurt more than surpluses help
  [@oliver1980; @anderson1993].
- Product attributes matter because they lead to **consequences and values**,
  and laddering reveals these chains [@gutman1982; @reynolds1988].
- **Brand equity** is a differential response to marketing that originates in
  brand knowledge, and it should be measured against a benchmark
  [@keller1993; @aaker1991].
- Brands acquire **personalities** and become **relationship partners** whose
  transgressions, norms, and attachment shape loyalty [@aaker1997;
  @fournier1998; @park2010].
- Consumers prefer brands that fit their **self-concept**, and possessions
  become part of an **extended self** [@sirgy1982; @belk1988].
- **Moderate incongruity** with a schema can be an advantage, but only when
  consumers can resolve it and risk is low [@meyerslevy1989; @campbell2001].
- **Hedonic** consumption requires justification, so effort, prior virtue, and
  charity tie-ins change choices [@dhar2000; @okada2005; @khan2006].
- **Psychological ownership** and **variety seeking** explain valuation and
  switching beyond price and quality [@pierce2001; @simonson1990].
- Prices are judged against **reference prices**, and promotions reshape those
  standards [@winer1986; @mazumdar2005].
- **Consumer culture theory** treats consumption as meaning-making that firms
  shape but do not control [@mccracken1986; @arnould2005].
:::

## Discussion Questions {#consumer-behavior-questions}

1. A hotel chain's satisfaction scores fall after a successful advertising
   campaign while service quality is unchanged. Use expectancy-disconfirmation
   theory to explain the pattern and design a study to test your explanation.
2. Conduct three short laddering interviews about a product you recently bought.
   Draw a hierarchical value map. Which level of the ladder offers the best
   positioning opportunity, and why?
3. Keller defines brand equity as a *differential* response. Design a study that
   measures brand equity for a national brand of breakfast cereal at the
   customer-mindset and product-market levels. What benchmark will you use?
4. Aaker, Fournier, and Brasel found that sincere and exciting brands respond
   differently to transgressions. How should a crisis communication plan differ
   for the two kinds of brands? State a testable hypothesis.
5. Choose a brand extension announced in the past five years. Predict its
   success using schema congruity theory and the drivers identified by Völckner
   and Sattler. What evidence would falsify your prediction?
6. A retailer plans to cut its promotion frequency in half. Using reference price
   theory, forecast the short-run and long-run effects on sales and perceived
   value, and explain how you would separate loss aversion from consumer
   heterogeneity in the data.

## Further Reading {#consumer-behavior-reading}

- @oliver1980: the classic statement of expectancy-disconfirmation and the
  starting point for satisfaction research.
- @keller1993: the foundational definition of customer-based brand equity and
  its memory-based logic.
- @aaker1997: the brand personality scale, best read together with the critique
  in @azoulay2003.
- @fournier1998: the paper that legitimised the study of consumer-brand
  relationships, rich in qualitative detail.
- @meyerslevy1989: a compact and elegant test of schema congruity with a clear
  mechanism.
- @mazumdar2005: the most comprehensive review of reference price research,
  with testable propositions.
- @arnould2005: the map of consumer culture theory and its research programmes.
- @alba2013: a review of hedonic consumption that connects the
  hedonic-utilitarian distinction to broader research on pleasure.
